records.doctrine_name: Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy

legal_basis.doctrine_basis: An employer's traditional right to discharge an at-will employee is limited by public policy. California recognizes a tort claim when an employer discharges an employee in contravention of a fundamental public policy tethered to constitutional, statutory, or regulatory law. In whistleblower settings, the doctrine protects employees fired for refusing illegal conduct, reporting employer wrongdoing, or raising safety concerns.
legal_basis.recognition_status: Well-established since the 1980 Tameny decision. Covers whistleblower retaliation when discharge contravenes a fundamental public policy. California courts bar Tameny claims against public entities, and it does not extend to independent contractors.
legal_basis.protected_class_details: Applies to employees in private employment relationships. Does not extend to independent contractors or public-entity defendants.
legal_basis.disclosure_targets_details: Depending on the underlying public policy and facts, California cases recognize protection for internal reporting to supervisors or management, external reporting to government or law-enforcement authorities, or refusal to participate in unlawful conduct.
legal_basis.adverse_action_scope: Strictly limited to termination or constructive discharge. Does not apply to demotions or other adverse actions short of termination.

statute_of_limitations.limit_details: Derived from Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 335.1, which provides a two-year period for personal injury actions and other torts. Earlier cases applied the former one-year period under § 340(3).
statute_of_limitations.trigger: Date of the termination or constructive discharge.

enforcement.remedies_details: Tort remedies including compensatory damages (lost wages, emotional distress), punitive damages where malice is shown, and equitable relief such as reinstatement in some applications.

burden_of_proof.statutory_preclusion_details: California courts generally hold that statutory remedies (like Lab. Code § 1102.5) are cumulative and do not preclude a common law Tameny claim.
burden_of_proof.burden_of_proof_details: Plaintiff must establish a causal link between the protected activity/refusal and the termination. The employee must show the protected activity was a substantial motivating reason for the adverse action.
